commentBody: Just a plain and fun Wednesday with no hiccups.
Very cute, and the story of my life.
Finally a nice puzzle this week. Monday and Tuesday had a few bad crosses, but today was a good fill even though it took me longer than my average Wednesday. The theme was also fun today.
I guess I'll be the first person to comment that Chicago's transit systems calls its trains "L" and not "EL." The "L" moniker dates back to the 1890s.
Too easy.

I thought this puzzle was PEACHYKEEN.  I got all three theme answers before seeing the revealer and was unsure what I was missing that dictated that all the responses reflect an inability to hear the speaker.  And then, voila, the revealer supplied the missing element that made the answers something other than random choices. I liked that, but I might have hated it if the answers hadn’t been easily deduced from a few crosses.

Jim Horne's only comment on xwordinfo.com was "Relatable theme."

I had the opposite reaction.  I retired in 2016, but continued to do some work for the school I last worked at for several years.  When the pandemic hit, remote work was not ready for prime time, but it had to done anyway, with Zoom, Google Teams, etc. being used extensively.

I only had a few involvements with these remote meetings, and rarely with large groups, so I didn't experience these issues as much as many others did.  And then, I was "encouraged" to come back in again, and I realized that it wasn't cost-effective anymore.  My commute had become two hours a day for typically four or five hours at work.

So I stopped working altogether.  And I don't miss it.  And I can't really relate to the theme, although it was a fine one, and I'm sure  loads of other people can.
Quick, clever and amusing.
@Sam. “Thou still unravished bride of quietness…” one of those lines just sticks in my memory. Have no idea, without looking it up, how the ode continues.

Maya civilization is absolutely not bygone! There are anywhere from 5 to 12 million Maya people still alive today, and it's still very much is a civilization. It really is inexcusable that this slipped by the editors. Editors. Lots of people have this mistaken belief that the Maya civilization and the Maya people suddenly disappeared more than a thousand years ago, and that is very much false.

Hmmm…Ok, I guess, but why the editors put this theme on a Wednesday instead of Monday or Tuesday I surely don’t know, especially after yesterday’s.

Let’s see, homophones or potential homophones seemed to be a secondary theme, we had SECTS/SEX and STU/STEW, was looking for RODE, PEAK, and PAIN ( as well as the less likely HAYES and BERRY.)

I’m glad the constructor did qualify WIZARDOFOZ because he was prominent in many other books. And, OK, I suppose he was behind the curtain for most of the first book but it still seems that such a lovely and unusual entry with two Z’s deserved a more interesting or noteworthy clue.

For the record, yes, I do say PEACHYKEEN all the time, or at least PEACHY.

I had to look up in what games ACES are wild. I’ve heard the phrase but never played one.

That’s about all I have to say. Nothing terribly negative about today’s “puzzle” but nothing really grabbed me.

Nor could I hear the others, and yes, the story ended with an OH FORGET IT.

Now, mind you, I love wordplay, I live for it, and I love that most crossword themes involve it, but I also love the refreshing contrast that comes with a non-wordplay theme, as Jacob gave us today, when he graced us with a mini-story.  

A relatable one for many, too, I’m guessing, either from the perspective of one who wasn’t heard in a virtual meeting, or who experienced participants who couldn’t be heard.

I also liked the good number of vague clues in the box today, such as [Hot stuff], [Tree with edible nuts], [Apartment option], [Look], [Dandy], and [Edit menu command].  That drew my brain in and got it doing the work it loves.

So thank you for the memory that I look back on with a smile, Jacob, and for a splendid outing today!

I am always a bit annoyed when clues for INCA and MAYA refer to “ancient civilizations” — since they are also contemporary people, the same way that OTOE, CREE, and UTES (other Indigenous crossword regulars, but north of the border!) are.

But “bygone” (1D) is both inaccurate and offensive. Contemporary Indigenous Maya people live today in southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, as well as large diaspora communities in the US and Canada. They make up a significant portion of the population of Guatemala, they speak around 30 different languages, and their cultures have survived despite centuries of colonial violence. 

I hope the editors can do a better job of not contributing to this erasure by using “ancient” and “bygone” cultures for contemporary people — in an otherwise enjoyable puzzle!

The Maya are far from a "bygone civilization". Mayans live now in many parts of Mesoamerica, and the continuities from the past into present Mayan culture are obvious. More are being documented all the time. I believe it was an article in this very publication (NYT) where I read that anthropology scholars are reconsidering the racist assumptions of past scholars who assumed anything as complex as Mayan culture couldn't be connected to the current day Mayans they met and disdained. They were wrong. Please don't add to the idea that Mayan civilization is a "bygone" phenomenon.

@SP It is not always considered a pronoun. Sometimes "possessive pronoun" is limited to theirs, hers, mine, ours, etc. and not their, her, my, our, etc.

To me, an interesting way to understand the motivation for having such a distinction is historical: in Old English, words like "my" were inflected like adjectives, instead of being treated like a noun in the genitive case. This is true e.g. in modern German as well.

However, relevant to the case at hand, third person possessives actually were the genitive case of the pronoun in Old English, just like in Latin (i.e., they were indisputably pronouns). So if anything, this strengthens the case for "their" being called a pronoun (although "their" actually comes from Norse, not Old English, it followed the same principle as far as I can tell).

I don't mean to imply that history need actually determine how we classify words, I just find it helps me to understand the potential difference between "possessive pronouns" and "determiners." I'm not an expert so I welcome any corrections.

@mld This doesn't bother me much, although it's hard to find much support for the NYT's apparently deliberate choice to insist that words like THEIR are possessive pronouns; most experts agree with you. But I have found one, a well-respected dictionary (Cambridge, that supports the Times): https://tinyurl.com/42bm6udv Cambridge calls both sets of possessives, the "my, your, THEIR" group, and the "mine, yours, theirs" group "pronouns," and then separates them into "possessive determiners" (the first group) and "possessive pronouns." The word "adjective" does not appear anywhere in this explanation. How we slice up words grammatically is often just a matter of tradition and convention. We say that pronouns replace nouns, and adjectives describe nouns (as well as pronouns). But what do you do about a word that both replaces a noun and modifies another noun? Consider: John and Mary wash cars. John and Mary wash John and Mary's cars. John and Mary wash their cars. In the first sentence, it is clear that the compound subject contains two nouns, John and Mary. The second repeats those names/nouns, one with a possessive marking attached, and uses them to specify whose cars they wash. In the third, the names are replaced by a shorter word. So "their" replaces two names (nouns) and also modifies another noun. So, is it a possessive pronoun, or a possessive adjective? (continued)

@Steve L Convention has been that the longer form (mine, theirs, etc.) are pronouns, and the shorter ones (my, their) are adjectives, but it doesn't have to be that way.
